title: Purists Rejoice: V-8s Return to F1 in 2030

body_markdown:
The FIA is steering Formula 1 regulations away from electrification and toward displacement. The governing body, the power unit manufacturers, and the teams that race in Formula 1 have unanimously agreed to bring back the V-8 starting in 2030. We previously reported that[V-8s would return in 2031](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/f1-will-return-to-v-8-power-by-2031/) , but things appear to be progressing quicker now, which is great for fans.


As of writing,[Formula 1 cars](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/watch-how-formula-1-cars-are-serviced-between-races/) use a power unit consisting of a turbocharged, 1.6-liter V-6 engine and a hybrid system. The new rules will ditch the six-cylinder in favor of a turbocharged, 2.1-liter V-8. Electrification isn’t going away entirely, though; the next power unit will feature hybrid assistance, but the FIA explains its goal is to end up with a system that features “limited hybridization.”


Mark Thompson/Getty Images


Interestingly, reigning in electrification and adding displacement is presented as a way to make the power units less complex, lighter, and cheaper to manufacture. FIA officials also hope that the V-8 will deliver “attack-oriented racing” and a fan-approved sound. The governing body remains conscious of the sport’s carbon footprint, however, and it announced that the next-generation power units will rely on “relevant and sustainable technology.” That likely means the engines will be configured to run on sustainable fuel.


Other regulatory updates that haven’t been detailed will change how teams design cars. “The plan is to marry the V-8 to a chassis which will also be lighter, more agile, and which will place greater emphasis on driver skill and close racing,” the FIA wrote.


FIA officials will present the final version of the 2030 Regulatory Framework to the FIA World Motor Sport Council during a meeting in Shanghai, China, in December 2026. Council members will need to approve all regulatory changes.


The V-8 isn’t new in Formula 1. Teams raced with a naturally aspirated, 2.4-liter V-8 between 2006 and 2013. The 90-degree eight-cylinder was celebrated for its screaming exhaust note and for its high redline (some early engines could reach over 20,000 rpm).


The post[Purists Rejoice: V-8s Return to F1 in 2030](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/formula-1-v-8-power-unit-2030-rules/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
